intro: Chachoengsao — or Paet Rio — is a riverside city on the Bang Pakong River that Bangkok people can drive to, pay respects at Luang Pho Sothon, and follow up with a great meal without any difficulty. From an old-school snakehead fish ho mok restaurant to pak mo noodles packed with fillings, riverside seafood, and a melon café in an orchard, we've gathered the 10 most talked-about spots and put them in one place. Take your pick for a main meal or dessert.

🍜 Pak mo noodles loaded with fillings

blocks.html:
Eating in Chachoengsao starts with the Bang Pakong River that flows through the center of the city — most of the standout restaurants cluster along this river. The old-town neighborhood near Wat Sothon is packed with ancient Thai restaurants and hidden gems in side streets that locals have been eating at for decades. Cross to the Tha Kham side and you find large riverside seafood houses open to the breeze. The Baan Mai 100 Pi market is a walking-and-eating neighborhood for snacks and a cup of coffee in old wooden shophouses. Drive further out toward Phanom Sarakham on Route 304 and you enter orchard country and melon cafés in the fields. The city has it all: bold savory food, cooling desserts, and water views good for a long sit.

Many restaurants on this list are names that Paet Rio locals stand behind. Pradit Phochana is an ancient Thai riverside restaurant that has been part of the city for so long that the snakehead ho mok always sells out before closing. Chai Khrap is a hidden spot in a soi near Wat Sothon, famous for its whole-fish-fried pla thu in fish sauce. For seafood, Eakkenok on the Bang Pakong side is known for its crab roe dipping sauce and crab meat lon. Baan Melon Desert is a desert-themed melon farm café where the melon bingsu brings people in for photos all the time. Every place on this list is actually open — scroll through all 10, then plan your meals.

blocks.name: Pradit Phochana
blocks.signature: Freshly steamed snakehead fish ho mok, pla kod na chu chi, fluffy crab omelette
blocks.descHtml:
Ask Paet Rio locals which restaurant is the riverside fixture of the Bang Pakong, and "Pradit Phochana" is consistently one of the first names out of their mouths. This single-story cream wooden house has stood on Maruphong Road for over 80 years, a grandmother's recipe handed down through generations. If you've just finished paying respects at Luang Pho Sothon and want a proper meal nearby, this is the spot — equally suited to families bringing the older generation along, and groups of friends who want to order multiple dishes and share.

The must-order is the snakehead fish ho mok — the restaurant's hero dish that regulars consistently describe as something to "order fast" because it sells out. Regular customers carry ten or twenty parcels home at a time. The fish is fresh and firm, the curry paste is rich and fragrant, and the bai yo leaves carry no bitterness. Another dish that draws a lot of praise is the pla kod na (catfish) chu chi — rounded and smooth without going overboard on the seasoning — alongside the fluffy crab omelette, airy and crispy, each bite full of crab. For something snacky, there's a classic crispy mee noodle, or you can try sun-dried beef and wild boar pad phet as well.

The atmosphere is relaxed home-style, open kitchen in plain sight, breezy seating, with a riverside section where the wind keeps things comfortable. Parking is available at a riverside lot. Prices run about 251–500 THB per person when sharing multiple dishes — fair for fresh river fish and river prawns.

Worth knowing: the restaurant only opens midday through evening (around 08:30–18:00 daily), and the ho mok typically sells out before closing time. If you're making a special trip for it, calling ahead to reserve ho mok parcels is the sensible move. Coming around late morning to early afternoon ensures the full menu is available and the wait won't be long.
blocks.bestFor: First meal in the province, after praying at Luang Pho Sothon

blocks.name: Kuayteaw Pak Mo Je Ju
blocks.signature: Pak mo noodles loaded with fillings, springy moo deng pork, house-made fish balls
blocks.descHtml:
After praying at Luang Pho Sothon and feeling your stomach start to rumble, this is the spot Paet Rio locals love to recommend. Kuayteaw Pak Mo Je Ju is a long-established institution in Chachoengsao, sitting on Sisothon Tad Mai Road for many decades. It's a relaxed wooden shophouse with rows of tables that fill up nearly every lunchtime. A great fit for anyone who's come to make merit and wants some genuinely local food at a very wallet-friendly price.

The hero of the restaurant is the pak mo itself, served on its own plate, 8 pieces per order, with a choice of fillings: garlic chives, bamboo shoots, tofu, cabbage, bean sprouts, long beans, and sweet preserved radish. Topped with crispy pork and fragrant fried garlic. The dough is very soft and chewy — it holds its shape in the hot soup without going mushy. You can eat it dry with dipping sauce or order it in soup, as you like. Reviewers consistently praise the broth: rounded and sweet, fragrant with simmered pork bone and a clear note of fried garlic.

Beyond the pak mo, other items to try are the boat noodles and moo deng tom yum — the house-made fish balls bounce as the name suggests. Heavier eaters can alternate with grilled pork neck rice or grilled chicken rice. Price per head is under 100 THB, a bowl of pak mo starting around 60 THB — good value for something made fresh to order.

Worth knowing: the restaurant opens daily around 09:30–16:30 (Sat–Sun 10:00–16:00). If it sells out, it closes early — arriving in the late afternoon risks missing the dishes you came for. Street parking is available in front. At lunchtime there may be a short wait since each bowl is made fresh, but waiting for something hot and just-cooked is absolutely worth it.
mustOrder: Pak mo noodles loaded with fillings (8 pieces)
blocks.bestFor: Lunch after praying at Luang Pho Sothon

blocks.name: Chai Khrap
blocks.signature: Fresh pla thu fried in fish sauce — eat the whole fish — pla thu yam with pennywort, dry massaman with young pork rib
blocks.descHtml:
If you've come to pray at Luang Pho Sothon and want a proper meal without dressing up, "Chai Khrap" is the restaurant Paet Rio locals love to bring people to. It's an old house that the owner converted into a Thai restaurant, with an air-conditioned indoor room and a shady garden section outside with trees and a fish pond — it feels more like eating at a friend's home than visiting a restaurant. The ideal spot for families or groups of friends who want to sit and talk for a long time. The name comes from the owner Hia Chai's nickname, someone who selects ingredients himself and has been open long enough to become a neighborhood staple.

The dish every table orders is the fresh pla thu fried in fish sauce — fried until so crispy you can eat the whole fish from head to bones, finished with a sweet-salty fish sauce that hits just right. Another dish with a lot of mentions is the pla thu yam with pennywort, tangy and bold, a great foil to the richness, alongside dry massaman with young pork ribs where the meat is tender and the curry paste is fragrant. For bold flavors, try the crab roe nam prik and lotus stem pad kapi. These are the menu items that reviews confirm are as good as the reputation suggests.

Prices are mostly around 70–240 THB per dish, average per person in the low hundreds — good value for the quantity and quality. Some reviews are candid that on weekends the wait can be long since the kitchen works fresh, and parking in the soi is fairly limited. Budget extra time if you're coming at peak hours.

The restaurant is in Prachasan soi, Na Mueang subdistrict — not far from Wat Sothon, but tucked deep in a soi. Watch for the Chai Khrap sign. Open daily 10:30–21:30. The kitchen closes slightly before the restaurant. If you want the special shrimp with glass noodles dish, calling ahead to reserve it is the safer play.
mustOrder: Fresh pla thu fried in fish sauce (eat the whole fish)
Dry massaman with young pork rib
blocks.bestFor: Family meal after praying at Luang Pho Sothon

blocks.name: Baan Mai Rim Nam Paet Rio
blocks.signature: River prawn in tamarind sauce, crab meat curry with curry powder, oyster omelette, tom yum
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to eat by the Bang Pakong River in an atmosphere that feels like stepping back forty or fifty years, Baan Mai Rim Nam Paet Rio is the restaurant Paet Rio locals love to show friends from out of town. The building is a nearly century-old wooden house, originally an old-city hotel, gradually converted by the owner into a restaurant while preserving most of the wooden furniture, wooden floors, and original character. Old music plays softly in the background. There's a riverside section open to the breeze and a comfortable indoor section. Ideal for people touring the old town of Chachoengsao, walking the Baan Mai 100 Pi market, then stopping for something good to eat.

The dish that comes up at nearly every table is large river prawns — either charcoal-grilled, with firm meat and naturally sweet roe, or the prawn in tamarind sauce, fried over controlled heat then covered in a sweet-sour sauce. Another quickly-sold dish is the crab meat curry with curry powder, and the oyster omelette where plump oysters are chosen, stir-fried until fragrant in the wok, crispy outside and soft inside. The tom yum here gets praised for not being sharp-sour or aggressively spicy — the clear broth is rounded and smooth, the fresh snapper free of any off-smell. Vegetable lovers should try the Baan Mai water morning glory over high heat and the fresh prawn gang liang.

Prices are fair for the generous portions — regular dishes start around 60 THB, large seafood dishes go up to 250–500 THB, and river prawns are priced by weight at roughly 1,400 THB per kilogram. Average per person comes to about 250–500 THB. Most reviews praise the food as good across the board, the view as pleasant, and the breeze as comfortable since the restaurant is open-air with no air conditioning.

Worth knowing: the restaurant is popular and busy. On weekends and at dinner you'll often have to queue and parking is fairly limited. Locals usually suggest arriving around 11am when the restaurant first opens to be more comfortable. Open daily 11:00–21:30. At 19–21 Panit Road, Na Mueang subdistrict, Mueang Chachoengsao — on the same street as the Baan Mai 100 Pi market, easy to combine the two.
mustOrder: Crab meat curry with curry powder
blocks.bestFor: Riverside lunch with family, combined with old-town sightseeing

blocks.name: Eakkenok Paet Rio
blocks.signature: Crab roe nam prik, crab meat lon, grilled river prawn, three-egg yam, stink bean with shrimp paste and shrimp
blocks.descHtml:
If you're driving into Mueang Chachoengsao from the Tha Kham side and are about to cross the bridge over the Bang Pakong, look carefully to your left and you'll find the large riverside restaurant that Paet Rio locals know well: "Eakkenok." This restaurant has been open for nearly ten years — a large Thai seafood house with hundreds of seats, an air-conditioned section, an open-air section facing the river, and private rooms for functions. Spacious parking. Great for large families, groups of friends, or anyone who wants a riverside meal close to Bangkok without a long drive.

The dish at nearly every table is the grilled river prawn — large, fat with sweet roe, the restaurant's signature. For crab lovers, don't miss the crab roe nam prik, promoted as a standout menu item, served with fresh vegetables (around 180 THB), alongside the crab meat lon with firm, generous flesh. Yam lovers should try the three-egg yam, combining crab roe, horseshoe crab roe, and fish roe tossed in a bold dressing (around 350 THB). And for a fragrant shrimp paste note, the stink bean with shrimp paste and shrimp goes extremely well with plain hot rice. Most reviews praise fresh ingredients, generous crab portions, and bold seasoning.

Prices fall in the mid-range, leaning slightly premium in the style of riverside seafood restaurants — around 250–500 THB per person. Large seafood items like river prawns are priced by weight; going as a group makes the order more worthwhile. Open daily 10:30–23:00. In the evening the atmosphere is perfect — cool breeze, a beautiful sunset over the river. One observation from reviews: mosquitoes can be present along the riverside at dusk — bringing repellent makes things more comfortable.

Eakkenok has maintained its reputation because it combines Bang Pakong river views, fresh ingredients, and a large capacity that can comfortably seat a crowd. Ideal for a family weekend meal, a celebration dinner, or bringing out-of-town guests to experience the best of Paet Rio. On holidays it gets busy — calling ahead to reserve a table is the comfortable approach.

blocks.name: Red Cat Cafe
blocks.area: Baan Mai 100 Pi market, Bang Pakong riverside, Mueang Chachoengsao District, Chachoengsao
blocks.signature: Longan Americano, Black Forest cake, homemade drinks and cakes
blocks.descHtml:
Red Cat Cafe is the legendary red cat café of the Baan Mai 100 Pi market in Chachoengsao. The restaurant is a two-story wooden house at the far end of the market, facing fully onto the Bang Pakong River. If you've been walking the old market until you're starting to feel the heat and want a cool riverside seat, this is exactly the right place — it's the only air-conditioned café in the market, and there's also an open riverside section for catching the breeze. Inside the café is decorated in cats everywhere: cat pillows, cat postcards, cat figurines in every corner — charming enough that kids and photography lovers are instantly at home.

The menu item people talk about most is the Longan Americano — black coffee blended with the sweet fragrant note of longan, refreshing in a way that doesn't exist elsewhere. Paired with the Black Forest cake that real reviewers describe as "delicious, not too sweet." Other homemade desserts include cookie and cream cake, cheesecake, mango mousse, and triple chocolate cake that gets praised for its fragrant cream cheese. Savory lovers can try a ham and cheese croissant — baked until crispy outside and soft inside, the right amount of everything. In short: both drinks and homemade bakery, everything in one place.

Prices are very accessible — drinks and cake start around 55 THB, average per person well under 100 THB. The atmosphere is the real selling point: sitting and sipping coffee while watching boats pass, the river breeze cool and quiet, relaxed — a corner to escape the noise that Bangkok day-trippers drive here specifically for. A Google score of 4.4 from several hundred reviews reflects that most people leave happy with both the coffee, the sweets, and the view.

Worth knowing before you go: the café only opens Saturday–Sunday and public holidays, around 8:30 through evening. Closed on weekdays. When it gets busy it can be a longer wait since the café is not large. Park near Wat Chin Pracha Samosorn (look for the AIS Fiber sign), walk into the market and turn right to the far end of the riverside — the red cat café will be waiting.
blocks.bestFor: Relaxed riverside sit, café lovers, visiting the old market on weekends

blocks.name: Baan Melon Desert
blocks.signature: Melon bingsu, fresh melon, melon smoothie, Parma ham and melon
blocks.descHtml:
If you're driving Route 304 Chachoengsao–Kabin Buri around kilometer 120 at Khao Hin Son subdistrict, Phanom Sarakham District, and you see a vivid orange building with giant cacti and a giant melon outside, that's Baan Melon Desert — a desert-themed melon farm café that has become a landmark of the area. The restaurant grows its own melon in a greenhouse out the back, so everything on the menu — savory food, desserts, and drinks — comes from their own melons. A great stop for families bringing children, photography lovers, and people driving through who want to pull over for something cold.

The most ordered item is the melon bingsu — soft milk-melon shaved ice, drizzled in melon-lemon sauce, topped with sliced fresh melon. Reviewers consistently say the melon is exceptionally sweet and juicy, around 155 THB a glass, big enough to share among two or three. The Parma ham and melon is fresh melon paired with salty ham in a satisfying contrast. Fresh whole melon can be eaten at the café or carried home. There's also a melon smoothie blended cold and refreshing, and for savory lovers the bacon and dried chili spaghetti or melon pani puri are options too.

Most people who come praise the desserts and drinks as better than the savory food. Reviews are candid that many people come purely for the melon and prefer the desserts over the pasta. The café space is wide — seating both inside in air-conditioning and outside — with a melon greenhouse and dwarf goats for kids to look at during the day, and cactus garden lighting at night that gives a different mood entirely. Easy parking and easy to pull in. Average spend around 400 THB per person.

Open daily from 10:30 (some periods closed Wednesdays — check their page before going). With a Google score of 4.8 from over 3,400 reviews, plus desert-themed photo spots hard to find anywhere else, this is one of the most popular stops along Route 304. Worth knowing: on holidays it gets busy with some queuing, and fresh melon is limited by harvest cycle — coming in the afternoon is the more relaxed option.
blocks.bestFor: Families with children + café and photo lovers stopping along Route 304
blocks.spice: Mostly not spicy (primarily desserts and melon)

blocks.name: Homnoir Somtum and Cafe
blocks.signature: Crispy pork corn tam, multi-style som tam, grilled chicken, coffee and bakery
blocks.descHtml:
If you're looking for a som tam restaurant that delivers both genuine bold flavor and a comfortable atmosphere to sit in, Homnoir somtum and café in Bang Phra has both in one place. The restaurant is a hybrid between a boldly-spiced Isan food spot and a clean minimalist white café — suited to people who want fiery tam followed by coffee or cake in a cool air-conditioned room. Good for families, groups of friends, or couples, since there's both a glass-wall air-conditioned section and several pretty photo corners.

The dish most talked about is the crispy pork corn tam, around 109 THB — sweet corn tossed in a rich dressing with crispy pork that's fried to a crisp without being hard. Another big seller is the Luang Prabang som tam, with a full fermented fish aroma, genuine Isan-style — that crowd will love it. For chicken lovers there are crispy fish-sauce chicken wings scattered with kaffir lime leaves, northern Isan-style laab with the flavor of someone who actually eats it that way, as well as glass-noodle tam with pork cracklings, oyster yam with full garnishes, and to close out: coffee, smoothies, and bakery like taro coconut milk custard cake. Reviews generally praise the tam as having strong, rounded flavors and a fermented fish sauce that's not too pungent.

Per-person spend is around 150–300 THB; ordering multiple shared dishes pushes it up, but represents good value for the food quality and atmosphere. Standout points that reviewers mention: food comes out quickly, good service, and wide parking. Located at Bang Phra subdistrict, in Klong Lad Yai Rang 1 soi, on the way to Wat Bang Prong, Mueang Chachoengsao. Open 10:00–21:00, closed every Tuesday. Worth knowing: many Isan dishes contain fermented fish sauce — if you don't eat it, tell the staff in advance. Weekend lunchtimes are busy — arriving early gets you a comfortable seat.
blocks.bestFor: Som tam lovers who want a relaxed café sit — groups and families
blocks.spice: Spice adjustable (many Isan dishes contain fermented fish sauce)

blocks.name: Krua Pla Thuean Sukprayoon 12
blocks.area: Sukprayoon 12 soi, Bang Tin Pet subdistrict, Mueang Chachoengsao District, Chachoengsao 24000
blocks.cuisine: Thai food — river fish and seafood
blocks.signature: Garlic-fried pla ma, fresh-grilled Bang Pakong river prawn
blocks.descHtml:
If you're looking for the real river fish restaurant of Paet Rio, Krua Pla Thuean is the name that locals pass along by word of mouth. The restaurant is tucked at the end of Sukprayoon 12 soi in Mueang Chachoengsao — follow it all the way to the end and you'll find an open breezy wooden house on the Bang Pakong River, with a cool breeze blowing all day and a wide view of the slow current. The kind of atmosphere where you eat and lose track of time. Suited to family meals on weekends, family gatherings, or bringing someone you like to watch the sunset.

The heart of the restaurant is the freshness of the ingredients — fish and shrimp come directly from the Bang Pakong River, live. Over 70 varieties of fish are available depending on the season: pla ma, pla nuea on, pla khao, pla bu, and unusual river fish hard to find in the city. The dish you can't miss is the large garlic-fried pla ma, with firm sweet flesh fragrant from crispy fried garlic, and the fresh grilled Bang Pakong river prawn — shells beautifully red, roe perfectly rich, dipped in bold seafood sauce and the combination speaks for itself.

There are more standout dishes to order in rotation: steamed pla bu in soy sauce with silky tender flesh, sour soup with fish and pickled bamboo shoots — a tangy rounded flavor, chu chi pla cha-on, bouncy fried shrimp cakes, and fragrant sun-dried squid. The cooking style is bold home-kitchen flavors, everything cooked fresh to order. Prices are accessible given the freshness and size of the ingredients — which is why Paet Rio locals keep coming back.

Krua Pla Thuean is open daily from mid-morning from 10:30 through evening. On holidays it gets fairly full — calling ahead to reserve a riverside table is the comfortable approach. Another destination worth adding to your itinerary if you visit Chachoengsao and want fresh river fish in a relaxed Bang Pakong riverside setting — this restaurant delivers on that exactly.
mustOrder: Fresh grilled Bang Pakong river prawn
Steamed pla bu in soy sauce
Sour soup with fish and pickled bamboo shoots
blocks.bestFor: Family meal and fresh river fish by the Bang Pakong

blocks.name: Kuayteaw Pak Mo Je Tim
blocks.signature: Original-recipe pak mo noodles — thin soft dough, rich broth, loaded fillings
blocks.descHtml:
If you're passing through Phanom Sarakham and want to try local food that's hard to find elsewhere, Kuayteaw Pak Mo Je Tim is the first stop that people in the area bring out-of-town friends to. The restaurant is in the old Tha Kwian market neighborhood, right at the entrance to the temple — a traditional two-story wooden house with the feel of the market from another era. Open since 1967, passed down to the second generation. The selling point is the "pak mo" — thin soft dough that Je Tim stuffs with all fillings herself, then serves one piece at a time into your bowl right in front of you, a sight rarely seen at an ordinary noodle shop.

The must-order is the pak mo with all fillings, with 7 filling choices: bean sprouts, bamboo shoots, garlic chives, long beans, corn, stir-fried tofu, and sweet filling. Add springy moo deng pork and fish balls for a well-filled bowl. People who've been before consistently say the pork bone broth is gently sweet and rounded without the seasoning overpowering the dough — the thin soft pak mo dough is the hero of the bowl, the moo deng pork bouncy as the name suggests. It's an easy, satisfying, home-style flavor.

Prices are friendly — mostly around 70–100 THB per bowl depending on added fillings. Good value for something made fresh. The atmosphere is a simple local restaurant. At lunchtime it gets busy but turns over quickly since it's semi-self-service. The restaurant opens daily in the late morning through afternoon, around 10:00–15:00. If you're making a specific trip for this, arriving before early afternoon is the safer bet since items sell out on some days.

This restaurant stays on the list of places people think of when Phanom Sarakham pak mo comes up because it's the original — maintaining the same recipe and serving style for decades. Suited to people who want genuine local food rather than a pretty-decorated shop. Worth knowing: the restaurant is in a soi inside the old market with limited parking — parking around the market and walking in is the comfortable approach.
blocks.bestFor: Midday local specialty lunch — the original pak mo

blocks.title: What to know before you eat in Chachoengsao

items.title: Getting around
items.text: Restaurants in Chachoengsao are spread across different areas: the old town on the riverbank, the Tha Kham side, and Phanom Sarakham which is further out. Renting a car or driving your own is the most flexible option. Grab is available in the town center but isn't as frequent as in Bangkok. The Baan Mai 100 Pi market neighborhood is easy to walk and eat.

items.title: Payment
items.text: Street stalls, pak mo noodle shops, and the old market primarily work on cash — carry small bills and change. Large seafood restaurants and cafés mostly accept PromptPay QR scan. Credit cards are not accepted everywhere, so having cash on hand is the safer approach.

items.title: Avoiding the rush
items.text: On weekends and long holidays, Bangkok people drive up to pray and sightsee in large numbers. Popular restaurants and cafés queue up at lunch through early afternoon. Coming before 11am or after 2pm is more comfortable. Popular items like the ho mok sell out quickly — order as soon as you sit down.

items.title: Tipping
items.text: Thai restaurants and street food don't require tipping. Leaving loose change is fine. At a seafood or café with full table service, a small tip of around 20–50 THB is a kind gesture.

items.title: Language and menus
items.text: Most local restaurants have Thai-only menus with limited English. A translation app or pointing at photos on the menu helps a lot. Large seafood restaurants and cafés sometimes have photo menus that make ordering easier.

items.title: Spice and riverside food
items.text: Thai food in this area can be boldly spiced — tell the staff "noi phet" (mild) if you can't take much heat. Seafood specialties like the crab roe nam prik and grilled river prawn are the signature items here. Ordering shared dishes to try multiple things is more rewarding.

blocks.title: Planning a full day of eating in Chachoengsao
blocks.html: If you're on a day trip, planning by location lets you eat at multiple restaurants without doubling back. Start the morning with praying at Luang Pho Sothon, then head into the old town for lunch — Pradit Phochana on the riverside or Chai Khrap, the hidden spot in a soi near Wat Sothon. Order the snakehead ho mok and the whole-fried pla thu early since both sell out fast. For an afternoon dessert, if you're staying in the city, stop at Red Cat Cafe at the Baan Mai 100 Pi market for a longan Americano with a riverside stroll. But if you're driving toward Phanom Sarakham, save Baan Melon Desert for the melon bingsu there instead. Close the evening with riverside seafood at Eakkenok on the Tha Kham side — order the crab roe nam prik and grilled river prawn, sit back with the Bang Pakong breeze. For pak mo lovers, both Je Ju and Je Tim serve a light, easy bowl — good as a between-meals snack, one bowl each, easy on the wallet.

blocks.text: After eating across Chachoengsao all day and not wanting a late-night drive back, find a stay in the town center near Wat Sothon and the Baan Mai market — easy to continue in the morning.

faq.q: Which restaurant is most famous in Chachoengsao?
faq.a: Depends which style you're after. For ancient Thai riverside food, Pradit Phochana is the name Paet Rio locals think of first — famous for a snakehead ho mok that sells out before closing. For the hidden-gem category, Chai Khrap near Wat Sothon is well-known for whole-fish-fried pla thu in fish sauce. For desserts, Baan Melon Desert in Phanom Sarakham is the melon café with the most reviews in the province.

The standouts are ancient Thai riverbank cuisine and seafood: snakehead ho mok, grilled river prawn, crab roe nam prik, and crab meat lon. Another local specialty is pak mo noodles — loaded with fillings — from both Je Ju and Je Tim. For dessert there's melon from the Phanom Sarakham orchards, made into bingsu and smoothies.

faq.q: How much does eating in Chachoengsao cost?
faq.a: Flexible depending on the restaurant. Pak mo noodle bowls run around 60–100 THB. Thai restaurants like Chai Khrap shared across the table come to about 100–250 THB per person. Large riverside seafood restaurants like Eakkenok and Baan Mai Rim Nam average around 250–500 THB per person. Café drinks and desserts are around 55–400 THB.

faq.q: Do I need to book restaurants in Chachoengsao ahead of time?
faq.a: Street stalls and pak mo shops are walk-in — no reservation needed. For large riverside seafood houses like Eakkenok or Baan Mai Rim Nam on weekends and long holidays when it's busy, calling ahead to reserve a riverside table is the safer move. Popular cafés like Baan Melon Desert on weekend afternoons also get crowded.

faq.q: Which places are open in the evening or late?
faq.a: Most riverside seafood restaurants are open into the evening. Eakkenok opens around 10:30–23:00 — ideal for a riverside dinner. Baan Melon Desert opens through around 9pm (closed Wednesdays). Thai daytime restaurants and pak mo shops generally close in the evening. If you're planning a main dinner, check individual opening hours before you go.
